gmat-focus-readiness-check-001.prompt: A coat listed at $160 is marked down 30%, and the reduced price is then cut another 10%. What is the price a customer pays?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-001.explanation: Sequential discounts multiply remaining-price factors: 160 × 0.70 × 0.90 = 100.80. The second 10% applies to $112, not to the original $160, so the customer pays $100.80.

distractorExplanations.a: Adds the two discounts into one 40% cut (160 × 0.60 = 96); the 10% applies to the already-reduced $112, not to the list price.
distractorExplanations.c: Takes only the first 30% markdown (160 × 0.70 = 112) and never applies the extra 10%.
distractorExplanations.d: Applies only the second 10% to list (160 × 0.90 = 144) and skips the 30% markdown.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-002.prompt: A cohort of 36 interns is split between juniors and seniors in the ratio 4:5. How many seniors are in the cohort?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-002.explanation: The 4:5 split makes 9 parts. Each part is 36 ÷ 9 = 4 interns, so seniors are 5 × 4 = 20. Equivalently, seniors are (5/9) × 36 = 20.

distractorExplanations.a: Counts the junior share (4/9 × 36 = 16) instead of the senior 5-part share.
distractorExplanations.b: Splits the cohort evenly (36 ÷ 2); a 4:5 ratio gives seniors more than half.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats 36 as the junior count and scales by 5/4; 36 is the whole cohort, which covers all 9 parts.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-003.prompt: Priya is now three times as old as Noah. In 8 years, Priya will be twice as old as Noah. How old is Noah now?

options.a: 8 years
options.b: 16 years
options.c: 24 years
options.d: 32 years

gmat-focus-readiness-check-003.explanation: Let Noah’s age be N, so Priya is 3N. Then 3N + 8 = 2(N + 8). Expanding gives 3N + 8 = 2N + 16, so N = 8. Check: ages 8 and 24 become 16 and 32, and 32 is twice 16.

distractorExplanations.b: Ages Noah but not Priya: 3N = 2(N + 8) gives N = 16, but Priya also gets 8 years older.
distractorExplanations.c: Reports Priya’s current age (3 × 8 = 24), not Noah’s age as asked.
distractorExplanations.d: 32 is Priya’s age 8 years from now, not Noah’s current age.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-004.prompt: Faucet P can fill a tank in 9 hours and faucet Q can fill the same tank in 18 hours. If both run together at constant rates, how long do they take to fill the tank?

options.a: 4.5 hours
options.b: 6 hours
options.c: 13.5 hours
options.d: 27 hours

gmat-focus-readiness-check-004.explanation: Combined rate is 1/9 + 1/18 = 2/18 + 1/18 = 3/18 = 1/6 tank per hour, so the time is 6 hours. Work problems add rates; they do not average the two times.

distractorExplanations.a: Halves P’s solo time (9 ÷ 2) as if Q were as fast as P; Q adds only 1/18 tank per hour.
distractorExplanations.c: Averages 9 and 18; two faucets working together finish faster than the faster faucet alone.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the two solo times; rates add when both run, so the time must fall below 9 hours.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-005.prompt: How many kilograms of an 8% salt brine must be mixed with 12 kg of a 20% salt brine to produce a 14% salt brine?

options.a: 6 kg
options.b: 12 kg
options.c: 24 kg
options.d: 40 kg

gmat-focus-readiness-check-005.explanation: Let x be kilograms of 8% brine. Salt balance: 0.08x + 0.20(12) = 0.14(x + 12). Then 0.08x + 2.4 = 0.14x + 1.68, so 0.72 = 0.06x and x = 12. Check: 0.96 + 2.4 = 3.36 salt in 24 kg, which is 14%.

distractorExplanations.a: Divides 0.72 by 0.12 (20% − 8%) instead of by 0.06 (14% − 8%), dividing by the wrong percent gap.
distractorExplanations.c: Reports the total mass of the final mixture (12 + 12), not the amount of 8% brine added.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaves the 12 kg out of the final mass: 0.08x + 2.4 = 0.14x gives 40, but the 20% brine is part of the mix.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-006.prompt: A lab has 7 chemists and 5 biologists. How many 4-person panels have exactly 2 biologists?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-006.explanation: Choose 2 biologists from 5 and 2 chemists from 7: C(5,2) × C(7,2) = 10 × 21 = 210. Order inside the panel does not matter, so combinations, not permutations, apply.

distractorExplanations.a: Chooses the 2 biologists but only one chemist (10 × 7), filling just 3 of the 4 seats.
distractorExplanations.c: Counts panels with at least 2 biologists (210 + 70 + 5); the stem says exactly 2.
distractorExplanations.d: C(12, 4) counts every 4-person panel and ignores the exactly-2-biologists condition.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-007.prompt: If n is a positive integer and 45n is a perfect square, what is the smallest possible n?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-007.explanation: 45 = 3² × 5. For 45n to be a square, every exponent in the prime factorization must be even, so n must supply one factor of 5. The least such n is 5, and 45 × 5 = 225 = 15².

distractorExplanations.a: n = 3 yields 135 = 3³ × 5, which still has odd exponents on 3 and on 5, so it is not a square.
distractorExplanations.b: n = 4 = 2² yields 180 = 2² × 3² × 5, which still has an odd exponent on 5.
distractorExplanations.d: 15 = 3 × 5 works but is not smallest; the extra 3 is unnecessary because 45 already has 3².

gmat-focus-readiness-check-008.prompt: The mean of 8 scores is 12. After one score is dropped, the mean of the remaining 7 scores is 10. What score was dropped?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-008.explanation: The original sum is 8 × 12 = 96. The remaining sum is 7 × 10 = 70. The dropped score is 96 − 70 = 26. Means convert to totals before subtracting.

distractorExplanations.a: Repeats the new mean instead of subtracting the two totals.
distractorExplanations.b: Finds the 7 × 2 = 14 shift in the remaining total but forgets to add the old mean of 12.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses 12 + 6 × 2, counting six remaining scores instead of seven.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-009.prompt: A refinery blends 70-purity lots with 40-purity lots to hit 52-purity. If the blend uses 6 lots of 40-purity, how many 70-purity lots are required?

options.a: 4 lots
options.b: 6 lots
options.c: 9 lots
options.d: 10 lots

gmat-focus-readiness-check-009.explanation: Let x be the number of 70-purity lots. Then 70x + 40(6) = 52(x + 6). So 70x + 240 = 52x + 312, hence 18x = 72 and x = 4. Check: 280 + 240 = 520 purity-units in 10 lots, or 52 each.

distractorExplanations.b: Matches the 6 lots of 40-purity, as if a 1:1 mix reached 52; a 1:1 mix averages 55.
distractorExplanations.c: Inverts the gaps: the ratio of 70-lots to 40-lots is 12:18, not 18:12, so 6 × 3/2 = 9 is backwards.
distractorExplanations.d: 10 is the total number of lots in the blend (4 + 6), not the number of 70-purity lots.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-010.prompt: A drawer holds 5 tagged chips and 11 untagged chips. Two chips are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability both are tagged?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-010.explanation: P(first tagged) = 5/16 and P(second tagged | first tagged) = 4/15. The product is 20/240 = 1/12. Without replacement, the second factor uses 15 chips, not 16.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats the draws as with replacement: (5/16)² = 25/256. Without replacement the second draw is 4/15.
distractorExplanations.c: Keeps 5 tagged chips for the second draw (5/16 × 5/15); one tagged chip is already gone.
distractorExplanations.d: Stops after the first draw (5/16) and never multiplies by 4/15.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-011.prompt: Solve the displayed exponential equation for x.
gmat-focus-readiness-check-011.explanation: Rewrite 9 = 3² and 27 = 3³ so 3^{2(x−1)} = 3^{3(x−3)}. Equal bases imply 2x − 2 = 3x − 9, hence x = 7. Check: 9^6 = (3²)^6 = 3^{12} and 27^4 = (3³)^4 = 3^{12}.

distractorExplanations.a: Swaps the powers, writing 3(x − 1) = 2(x − 3); 9 is 3² and 27 is 3³.
distractorExplanations.b: Distributes the power only to x on one side: 2x − 2 = 3x − 3 drops the factor 3 on the constant.
distractorExplanations.c: Multiplies only the x terms by the powers: 2x − 1 = 3x − 3 leaves both constants undistributed.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-012.prompt: What is the value of $2,500 after 2 years at 8% interest compounded annually?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-012.explanation: Compound amount is 2500 × (1.08)² = 2500 × 1.1664 = 2916. The second year earns 8% on 2700, which is 216, for a two-year total of 416 above principal.

distractorExplanations.a: $416 is the interest earned over two years; the stem asks for the account value.
distractorExplanations.b: Applies 8% for only one year (2,500 × 1.08 = 2,700) and stops.
distractorExplanations.c: Computes simple interest for two years (2,500 × 0.08 × 2 = 400), skipping interest on the first year’s interest.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-013.prompt: If 3x + y = 17 and x − y = 3, what is the value of x?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-013.explanation: Add the equations: (3x + y) + (x − y) = 17 + 3, so 4x = 20 and x = 5. Then y = 2 from x − y = 3. Check: 3(5) + 2 = 17.

distractorExplanations.a: 2 is the value of y from x − y = 3; the question asks for x.
distractorExplanations.b: Adds the left sides but subtracts the right sides (17 − 3 = 14), so 4x = 14.
distractorExplanations.d: Subtracting the equations gives 2x + 2y = 14, so x + y = 7, not x.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-014.prompt: An arithmetic sequence begins 11, 17, 23, 29, … with constant difference 6. What is the 10th term?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-014.explanation: The nth term is 11 + (n − 1) × 6. For n = 10 that is 11 + 9 × 6 = 11 + 54 = 65. The 10th term uses nine steps from the first term, not ten.

distractorExplanations.a: Computes the 9th term: 11 + 8 × 6 = 59, an off-by-one on the number of steps.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses ten steps (11 + 10 × 6 = 71) as if a_n = a_1 + n d.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses eleven steps (11 + 11 × 6 = 77), shifting the index two places.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-015.prompt: k is a positive integer such that 4k leaves remainder 5 when divided by 7. What is the smallest possible k?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-015.explanation: The condition is 4k ≡ 5 (mod 7). The inverse of 4 modulo 7 is 2 because 4 × 2 = 8 ≡ 1. Multiply both sides by 2: k ≡ 10 ≡ 3 (mod 7). The least positive k is 3, and 4 × 3 = 12 = 7 × 1 + 5.

distractorExplanations.a: k = 1 gives 4, which leaves remainder 4 modulo 7, not 5.
distractorExplanations.b: 2 is the inverse of 4 modulo 7 (4 × 2 ≡ 1), a step toward the answer, not the solution of 4k ≡ 5.
distractorExplanations.d: Multiplies 5 by the inverse 2 to get 10 but never reduces modulo 7; 10 ≡ 3, and 4 × 10 = 40 leaves remainder 5 but is not smallest.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-016.prompt: A courier drives 120 km at 40 km/h and then 80 km at 80 km/h. What is the average speed for the whole 200 km?

options.a: 40 km/h
options.b: 50 km/h
options.c: 56 km/h
options.d: 60 km/h

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-016.explanation: Time is 120/40 + 80/80 = 3 + 1 = 4 hours. Average speed is total distance over total time: 200/4 = 50 km/h. Do not average 40 and 80, because the legs take unequal time.

distractorExplanations.a: Reports only the slower leg’s speed, as if the whole trip ran at 40 km/h.
distractorExplanations.c: Weights each speed by distance ((120 × 40 + 80 × 80) ÷ 200); average speed must be weighted by time.
distractorExplanations.d: Averages 40 and 80 directly, ignoring that the 40 km/h leg takes three times as long.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-017.prompt: At a studio, 40% of staff are engineers, 35% are designers, and the rest are in QA. If 96 people are engineers, how many are in QA?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-017.explanation: Engineers are 40% of headcount, so total staff is 96 / 0.40 = 240. QA is 100% − 40% − 35% = 25% of 240, which is 60 people.

distractorExplanations.b: Takes the designer share (35% of 240 = 84) instead of the 25% QA share.
distractorExplanations.c: Copies the given engineer count rather than converting 25% of the 240 total.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses 50% of 240, as if QA were everyone outside engineering and design were ignored.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-018.prompt: A wholesaler marks an item 50% above cost, then sells it at 20% off that marked price. What is the profit as a percent of cost?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-018.explanation: Let cost be 100. The marked price is 150. After 20% off, the selling price is 150 × 0.80 = 120. Profit is 20 on a cost of 100, so 20%. The 50% and 20% cannot be subtracted as 30%.

distractorExplanations.a: Divides the $20 profit by the $120 selling price; the stem asks for profit as a percent of cost.
distractorExplanations.c: Subtracts the percents (50 − 20 = 30) instead of applying them in sequence to cost.
distractorExplanations.d: Applies the 20% discount to the 50% markup itself (50 × 0.80 = 40), not to the marked price.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-019.prompt: Three consecutive multiples of 3 add to 72. What is the largest of the three?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-019.explanation: Let the integers be n, n + 3, and n + 6. Then 3n + 9 = 72, so 3n = 63 and n = 21. The three multiples are 21, 24, and 27; the largest is 27. Check: 21 + 24 + 27 = 72.

distractorExplanations.a: Reports the smallest of the three (n = 21), not the largest.
distractorExplanations.b: Reports the middle multiple (24) instead of n + 6.
distractorExplanations.d: Steps one extra multiple of 3 past 27, as if the sum used n + 9 as the third term.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-020.prompt: Crew A installs 20 cabinets per hour and Crew B installs 30 cabinets per hour. Working together at those constant rates, how long will they take to install 250 cabinets?

options.a: 5 hours
options.b: 8⅓ hours
options.c: 10 hours
options.d: 12.5 hours

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-020.explanation: Rates of crews working at the same time add: 20 + 30 = 50 cabinets per hour. Time = work ÷ rate = 250 ÷ 50 = 5 hours. Check: in 5 hours Crew A installs 100 and Crew B installs 150, for 250 in total.

distractorExplanations.b: Uses only Crew B's 30 cabinets per hour (250 ÷ 30 ≈ 8⅓) and ignores Crew A's contribution to the joint rate.
distractorExplanations.c: Averages the two rates to 25 cabinets per hour and divides 250 ÷ 25 = 10, but crews working together add their rates.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses only Crew A's 20 cabinets per hour (250 ÷ 20 = 12.5), as if Crew B never joined the job.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-021.prompt: A grant rose 12% from Year 1 to Year 2, then fell 25% from Year 2 to Year 3. Year 3 funding was $84,000. What was Year 1 funding?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-021.explanation: Year 3 = Year 1 × 1.12 × 0.75 = Year 1 × 0.84. So Year 1 = 84,000 / 0.84 = 100,000. Net change is multiplicative (0.84), not 12% − 25% = −13% of the original.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses each step with the opposite percent (× 1.25, then × 0.88); each change is undone by dividing by its own factor.
distractorExplanations.c: Divides 84,000 by 0.75 only, undoing the 25% drop but not the earlier 12% rise.
distractorExplanations.d: Multiplies by 1.25 and by 1.12; the 25% drop is undone by ÷ 0.75, and the 12% rise by ÷ 1.12, not × 1.12.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-022.prompt: In a geometric sequence the third term is 12 and the sixth term is 96. What is the first term?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-022.explanation: If the first term is a and the ratio is r, then ar² = 12 and ar⁵ = 96. The quotient is r³ = 8, so r = 2. Then a(2)² = 12 gives 4a = 12 and a = 3. Check: 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 96.

distractorExplanations.a: Takes r = 8 from 96 ÷ 12, forgetting that three steps separate the 3rd and 6th terms, so r³ = 8.
distractorExplanations.b: Halves 8 to get r = 4 instead of taking the cube root of 8.
distractorExplanations.d: Divides 12 by r only once; the first term is two steps before the third, so divide by r².

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-024.prompt: 25% of m equals 40% of n, and m + n = 130. What is the smaller of m and n?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-024.explanation: From 0.25m = 0.40n, m = 1.6n. Then 1.6n + n = 130, so 2.6n = 130 and n = 50. Thus m = 80, and the smaller number is 50.

distractorExplanations.b: Takes 40% of 130, applying one of the equation’s percents to the sum instead of solving for n.
distractorExplanations.c: Splits 130 evenly, ignoring that 25% of m = 40% of n forces m to be larger than n.
distractorExplanations.d: Reports m = 80, the larger value, instead of the smaller n = 50.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-025.prompt: A vat holds 30 liters of a 10% juice mix. How many liters of pure juice must be added to make the mix 25% juice?

options.a: 3 liters
options.b: 4.5 liters
options.c: 6 liters
options.d: 7.5 liters

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-025.explanation: There are currently 3 liters of juice. After adding x liters of pure juice, (3 + x)/(30 + x) = 0.25. Then 3 + x = 7.5 + 0.25x, so 0.75x = 4.5 and x = 6. Check: 9 liters juice in 36 liters is 25%.

distractorExplanations.a: 3 L is the juice already in the vat, not the amount that must be added.
distractorExplanations.b: Keeps the total at 30 L: (3 + x) ÷ 30 = 0.25 gives 4.5, but adding juice also raises the volume.
distractorExplanations.d: 7.5 L is 25% of the original 30 L, the juice target if the volume stayed fixed, not the amount to add.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-026.prompt: A shop’s cost of making x units is C(x) = 100 + 12x + 0.1x² dollars. What is C(21) − C(20), the extra cost of the 21st unit?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-026.explanation: The difference is 12(21 − 20) + 0.1(21² − 20²) = 12 + 0.1(441 − 400) = 12 + 0.1 × 41 = 12 + 4.10 = 16.10. The quadratic term grows by 0.1 times the odd number 41, not by 0.1 alone.

distractorExplanations.a: Counts only the linear 12x term; the 0.1x² term also grows, from 40 to 44.10.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses the slope at x = 20 (12 + 0.2 × 20); the exact difference is 0.1 higher because 21² − 20² = 41.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses 21² − 20² = 42 instead of 41, giving 12 + 4.20 = 16.20.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-028.prompt: A fund holds stocks and cash. Stocks gain 10% and cash loses 6%; the whole fund then gains 4%. What is the ratio of stocks to cash?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-028.explanation: Let S and C be starting amounts. Then 0.10S − 0.06C = 0.04(S + C). So 0.10S − 0.06C = 0.04S + 0.04C, hence 0.06S = 0.10C and S/C = 10/6 = 5/3. The stocks-to-cash ratio is 5:3.

distractorExplanations.a: Inverts 5:3. A 3:5 mix would net 0.10(3) − 0.06(5) over 8, which is 0, not +4%.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses 10:6 simplified one step too far to 2:1, dropping the 5:3 reduction.
distractorExplanations.d: Matches the 10% and 4% figures as 10:4 = 5:2 instead of 0.06S = 0.10C.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-029.prompt: An inlet pipe can fill a cistern in 10 hours, and a drain can empty the full cistern in 15 hours. If both are opened with the cistern empty, how long until it is full?

options.a: 5 hours
options.b: 6 hours
options.c: 25 hours
options.d: 30 hours

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-029.explanation: Net rate is 1/10 − 1/15 = 3/30 − 2/30 = 1/30 cistern per hour, so the fill time is 30 hours. The drain subtracts from the inlet; the times are not added to 25 or averaged to 12.5.

distractorExplanations.a: Subtracts the times (15 − 10); times do not combine this way, rates do.
distractorExplanations.b: Adds the two rates (1/10 + 1/15), treating the drain as a second inlet.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds the two times; opposing rates subtract, giving a net 1/30 cistern per hour.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-030.prompt: What remainder does 2^10 leave when divided by 9?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-030.explanation: Powers of 2 modulo 9 cycle every 6: 2, 4, 8, 7, 5, 1. Since 10 ≡ 4 (mod 6), the remainder matches the 4th entry, 7. Directly, 2^10 = 1024 and 1024 = 9 × 113 + 7.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses cycle position 6 (remainder 1), as if 10 were a multiple of 6.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses 10 mod 4 = 2 and reports 2² = 4; powers of 2 modulo 9 repeat every 6, not every 4.
distractorExplanations.d: Finds 10 ≡ 4 (mod 6) but reports 2⁴ = 16 itself without reducing modulo 9.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-031.prompt: After a 20% discount, a buyer pays $152. What was the pre-discount price?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-031.explanation: The buyer paid 80% of list, so list = 152 / 0.80 = 190. Raising 152 by 20% (152 × 1.20 = 182.40) does not undo a 20% markdown, because that 20% was of the original, not of 152.

distractorExplanations.a: Takes another 20% off $152; the buyer paid 80% of list, so list = 152 ÷ 0.80.
distractorExplanations.b: Raises $152 by 20%; the 20% was taken off the original price, not off $152.
distractorExplanations.d: Divides by 0.20, the discount, instead of by 0.80, the share of list the buyer paid.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-032.prompt: A sequence satisfies a1 = 3 and a_{n+1} = 3a_n − 1. What is the fourth term?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-032.explanation: a2 = 3(3) − 1 = 8, a3 = 3(8) − 1 = 23, a4 = 3(23) − 1 = 68. Each step multiplies by 3 then subtracts 1; skipping the −1 on the last step would produce 69, not an option here.

distractorExplanations.a: Stops at a3 = 23, one iteration short of the fourth term.
distractorExplanations.c: Computes 3 × 24 − 1, using 24 in place of a3 = 23.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses 3 × 27 − 1, as if a3 were 27 (3³) instead of 23.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-034.prompt: A share price falls 10%, then rises 20%, then rises 25%. If the final price is $270, what was the starting price?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-034.explanation: The multipliers are 0.90 × 1.20 × 1.25 = 1.35. Starting price P satisfies 1.35P = 270, so P = 270 / 1.35 = 200. The three percent moves must be multiplied, not added to +35% of an unknown base.

distractorExplanations.a: Takes 35% off $270; a 35% net gain is undone by dividing by 1.35, not by subtracting 35% of the end price.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses each move with the opposite percent (× 0.75, × 0.80, × 1.10); each change is undone by dividing by its own factor.
distractorExplanations.d: Multiplies 270 by 1.35 instead of dividing, running the three changes forward again.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-035.prompt: In a cohort of 150 analysts, 90 take statistics, 70 take economics, and 40 take both. How many take neither course?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-035.explanation: By inclusion-exclusion, those in at least one course are 90 + 70 − 40 = 120. Neither is 150 − 120 = 30. Subtracting the overlap once prevents double-counting the 40 who take both.

distractorExplanations.b: 40 is the overlap (analysts taking both), not those outside both courses.
distractorExplanations.c: Subtracts the overlap twice (90 + 70 − 80 = 80 in a course), undercounting the union.
distractorExplanations.d: 80 is the number taking exactly one course (50 + 30), not the number taking neither.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-036.prompt: Tea bags come in packs of 10 and coffee pods in packs of 15. What is the smallest number of each that a buyer can purchase so the two counts are equal?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-036.explanation: The counts must be a common multiple of 10 and 15. The least common multiple is 2 × 3 × 5 = 30. That is 3 packs of tea and 2 packs of coffee. Any larger common multiple (60, 90) works but is not minimal.

distractorExplanations.b: Uses 3 × 15 but 45 is not a multiple of 10, so tea packs would not be whole.
distractorExplanations.c: A common multiple (LCM × 2) but twice the least equal count.
distractorExplanations.d: 90 is a common multiple (9 packs of tea, 6 of coffee) but three times the least common multiple.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-037.prompt: How many positive divisors does 60 have?

distractorExplanations.a: Adds the exponents (2 + 1 + 1) instead of multiplying the (exponent + 1) factors.
distractorExplanations.b: Drops the factor 5: (2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 6 counts the divisors of 12, not 60.
distractorExplanations.c: Excludes 1 and 60 itself; the question counts all positive divisors.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-038.prompt: A copy shop runs a four-hour overnight job. It prints 40 pages in the first hour, and each later hour it prints 8 more pages than the hour before. How many pages are printed in the four hours combined?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-038.explanation: The hourly counts form an arithmetic sequence 40, 48, 56, 64. The four-term sum is 4/2 × (first + last) = 2 × (40 + 64) = 208 pages. Equivalently, S = 4/2 × (2 × 40 + 3 × 8) = 2 × 104 = 208.

distractorExplanations.b: 216 would be the sum if the last hour were 72 (a fifth term), which is one hour past the four-hour window.
distractorExplanations.c: 224 treats the increase as 8 pages per hour added to a flat 40 × 4 = 160, giving 160 + 64 instead of summing the actual hourly totals.
distractorExplanations.d: 240 is 40 × 6, as if the shop printed at the opening rate for six hours rather than four increasing hours.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-039.prompt: A delivery van leaves a warehouse at 8:00 a.m. traveling 50 mph on a straight highway. A second van leaves the same warehouse at 9:00 a.m. along the same route at 70 mph. At what clock time does the second van first catch the first?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-039.explanation: By 9:00 a.m. the first van has a 50-mile head start. The second van closes that gap at 70 − 50 = 20 mph, so it needs 50/20 = 2.5 hours after 9:00 a.m., which is 11:30 a.m. Distance check: first van 50 × 3.5 = 175 miles; second van 70 × 2.5 = 175 miles.

distractorExplanations.a: 11:00 a.m. is only 2 hours after 9:00, which would close 40 miles, not the 50-mile head start.
distractorExplanations.c: 12:00 p.m. would be 3 hours of closing at 20 mph (60 miles), overshooting the actual 50-mile gap.
distractorExplanations.d: 12:30 p.m. treats the head start as 70 miles or uses the slower van’s speed as the closing rate.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-040.prompt: A grocer blends 12 kilograms of almonds priced at $8 per kilogram with 8 kilograms of cashews priced at $14 per kilogram. If the mix is sold with no extra markup, what is the price per kilogram of the blend?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-040.explanation: Total cost is 12 × 8 + 8 × 14 = 96 + 112 = $208. Total mass is 20 kilograms, so the blend price is 208/20 = $10.40 per kilogram. That is the mass-weighted average (12/20)(8) + (8/20)(14) = 4.80 + 5.60 = 10.40.

distractorExplanations.a: $10.00 is the simple average of $8 and $14, correct only if the two masses were equal.
distractorExplanations.c: Swaps the weights, pricing 8 kg at $8 and 12 kg at $14; the cheaper almonds are the larger share.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses 8/12 instead of 8/20 as the cashew weight: 8 + 6 × 8/12 = 12; the weight is cashews over the whole blend.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-041.prompt: An analyst is paid $20 per hour for the first 36 hours in a week and 1.5 times that hourly rate for each overtime hour. In a week with 8 overtime hours, what is the analyst’s total pay?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-041.explanation: Regular pay is 36 × 20 = $720. Overtime is paid at $30 per hour, so 8 × 30 = $240. Combined pay is 720 + 240 = $960. The 1.5 multiplier applies only to the 8 overtime hours, not to the whole 44-hour week.

distractorExplanations.a: $720 is regular pay only and omits the eight overtime hours entirely.
distractorExplanations.b: $800 treats overtime as $10 extra per hour on $720 (720 + 80) instead of paying $30 per overtime hour.
distractorExplanations.c: Pays the 8 overtime hours at the regular $20 rate (720 + 160) instead of $30.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-042.prompt: A warehouse stacks identical crates so that the number of crates n satisfies n² + n − 12 = 0. If n must be a positive integer, how many crates are in the stack?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-042.explanation: Factor n² + n − 12 = (n + 4)(n − 3) = 0, so n = −4 or n = 3. Only the positive integer n = 3 is admissible. Check: 3² + 3 − 12 = 9 + 3 − 12 = 0.

distractorExplanations.b: 4 is the absolute value of the negative root; substituting n = 4 gives 16 + 4 − 12 = 8, not 0.
distractorExplanations.c: 6 is the product of 3 and 2, not a root; 36 + 6 − 12 ≠ 0.
distractorExplanations.d: 12 is the constant term of the quadratic, not a solution of the equation.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-043.prompt: Consultant A can finish an audit alone in 12 workdays, and Consultant B can finish the same audit alone in 18 workdays. If they work together at those constant rates with no overlap or idle time, how many workdays does the audit take?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-043.explanation: A’s rate is 1/12 of the audit per day and B’s is 1/18. Combined rate is 1/12 + 1/18 = 3/36 + 2/36 = 5/36 of the audit per day, so the time is 36/5 = 7.2 workdays. The harmonic shortcut 12 × 18 / (12 + 18) = 216/30 = 7.2 confirms the same result.

distractorExplanations.b: Halves B’s 18 days, as if A worked at B’s pace; A is faster, so the pair beats 9 days.
distractorExplanations.c: Averages 12 and 18; working together, the pair finishes faster than A alone.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the two solo times; together the consultants finish faster than either one alone.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-044.prompt: A lab protocol dilutes a sample by a factor of 1/2 at each step. If the recorded concentration after four reverse (concentrating) steps is modeled by (1/2)^(−4) times the diluted reading, what is the numerical value of (1/2)^(−4)?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-044.explanation: A negative exponent inverts the base: (1/2)^(−4) = 2^4 = 16. Equivalently, four reverse dilutions each multiply by 2, so the scale factor is 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16.

distractorExplanations.a: Ignores the negative sign and computes (1/2)⁴ = 1/16, a dilution, not the reverse scale factor.
distractorExplanations.b: 4 equals the exponent, or 2², which would be (1/2)^(−2), two reverse steps rather than four.
distractorExplanations.c: 8 = 2³, the scale for three reverse steps, not four.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-045.prompt: A shipping code is the positive integer 360. How many distinct positive divisors does 360 have?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-045.explanation: Prime factorization is 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5¹. The divisor-count formula multiplies one plus each exponent: (3 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 distinct positive divisors.

distractorExplanations.a: Adds the exponents (3 + 2 + 1); the count multiplies the (exponent + 1) factors.
distractorExplanations.b: Counts the divisors of 60 (2² × 3 × 5) and misses the third factor of 2 in 360.
distractorExplanations.c: Factors 360 as 2² × 3² × 5, which is 180, giving 3 × 3 × 2 = 18.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-046.prompt: A contractor’s fee is $50,000. The client first raises the fee by 20% after a scope change, then cuts the new fee by 20% when part of the work is dropped. What is the fee after both adjustments?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-046.explanation: After the 20% increase the fee is 50,000 × 1.20 = $60,000. A 20% cut of that new amount is 60,000 × 0.80 = $48,000. Successive +20% and −20% multiply by 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, so the original fee falls by 4%, not back to itself.

distractorExplanations.b: $50,000 assumes a 20% raise and a 20% cut cancel; they do not, because the cut applies to the already increased base.
distractorExplanations.c: $52,000 adds a net 4% instead of subtracting the 4% compound loss.
distractorExplanations.d: $60,000 stops after the raise and never applies the later 20% reduction.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-047.prompt: The pair of equations 2x + 3y = 18 and 4x + 6y = k is to have infinitely many solutions in x and y. What must k equal?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-047.explanation: Infinitely many solutions require the second equation to be a scalar multiple of the first. Doubling 2x + 3y = 18 produces 4x + 6y = 36, so k must be 36. Any other k makes the lines parallel and distinct (no solution) rather than coincident.

distractorExplanations.a: 18 copies the first constant term and ignores that the left-hand coefficients were doubled.
distractorExplanations.c: 54 triples 18, but the coefficient ratio is 2, not 3 (4/2 = 6/3 = 2).
distractorExplanations.d: 72 quadruples 18, matching a factor of 4 that is not the ratio of the x- or y-coefficients.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-048.prompt: Pipe A can fill an empty tank in 10 minutes and Pipe B can fill it in 15 minutes. Pipe A runs alone for 4 minutes, and then Pipe B is also opened. How many more minutes until the tank is full?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-048.explanation: In 4 minutes A fills 4/10 of the tank, leaving 6/10. Together the pipes fill 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 tank per minute, so the rest takes (6/10) ÷ (1/6) = 3.6 minutes. Check: A adds 3.6/10 and B adds 3.6/15, which is 0.36 + 0.24 = 0.60.

distractorExplanations.a: Applies the joint rate to the 4/10 already filled (0.4 × 6) instead of to the 6/10 still empty.
distractorExplanations.c: 6 minutes is the joint time for a full empty tank; 4/10 of the tank was already filled by A.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses only Pipe B’s rate for the remaining 6/10 (0.6 × 15), forgetting that A keeps running.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-049.prompt: A loyalty-points sequence starts at 2 points. Each later week the balance is obtained by doubling the previous week’s points and then adding 1. What is the balance after four weeks, that is, the fourth term?

distractorExplanations.a: 11 is the third term; the stem asks for the fourth, one more doubling-plus-one beyond 11.
distractorExplanations.b: Adds 8 to 11 instead of doubling 11 and adding 1.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds 1 before doubling at each step (2 → 6 → 14 → 30); the rule doubles first, then adds 1.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-050.prompt: Two consecutive even positive integers have product 224. What is the larger of the two integers?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-050.explanation: Let the integers be n and n + 2 with n even. Then n(n + 2) = 224, so n² + 2n − 224 = 0. Trial of even factors of 224 shows 14 × 16 = 224. The larger integer is 16. Check: 16 − 14 = 2, both even.

distractorExplanations.a: 14 is the smaller of the two integers; the stem asks for the larger.
distractorExplanations.c: 18 is the next even integer after 16, but 16 × 18 = 288, not 224.
distractorExplanations.d: 28 × 8 = 224, but 28 and 8 are not consecutive even integers.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-051.prompt: Two production lots contain 84 units and 126 units. The lots will be split into identical smaller cartons with no units left over. What is the greatest carton size, in units, that works for both lots?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-051.explanation: The greatest common carton size is gcd(84, 126). Factor 84 = 2² × 3 × 7 and 126 = 2 × 3² × 7, so gcd = 2 × 3 × 7 = 42. Euclidean check: 126 = 1 × 84 + 42, and 84 = 2 × 42 + 0, remainder 0 at 42.

distractorExplanations.a: 14 divides both lots but is not greatest; 42 is a larger common divisor (84/42 = 2 and 126/42 = 3).
distractorExplanations.c: 84 divides 84 but not 126 (126/84 is not an integer), so leftover units would remain in the second lot.
distractorExplanations.d: 126 is the size of the larger lot; it does not divide 84.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-052.prompt: A cost split is written as 2x/5 + x/3 = 11, where x is the invoice amount in thousands of dollars. What is x?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-052.explanation: Multiply through by 15, the least common multiple of 5 and 3: 15 × (2x/5) + 15 × (x/3) = 165, which simplifies to 6x + 5x = 165, so 11x = 165 and x = 15. Check: 30/5 + 15/3 = 6 + 5 = 11.

distractorExplanations.a: x = 9 gives 18/5 + 3 = 3.6 + 3 = 6.6, well short of 11.
distractorExplanations.d: x = 18 gives 36/5 + 6 = 7.2 + 6 = 13.2, overshooting 11.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-053.prompt: A cafe surveyed 200 customers. 110 bought coffee, 90 bought pastry, and 40 bought both coffee and pastry. How many customers bought neither coffee nor pastry?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-053.explanation: Inclusion-exclusion: coffee or pastry = 110 + 90 − 40 = 160 customers. Neither = 200 − 160 = 40. The 40 who bought both are inside both counts, so they must be subtracted once to avoid double-counting.

distractorExplanations.a: Adds 110 + 90 = 200 without removing the 40 counted twice, so nobody seems left over.
distractorExplanations.c: Subtracts the overlap twice (110 + 90 − 80 = 120), undercounting those who bought something.
distractorExplanations.d: 120 bought exactly one item (70 coffee-only + 50 pastry-only), not neither.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-054.prompt: A hashing check stores 2^10 as an integer and then reports the remainder when that integer is divided by 11. What remainder is reported?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-054.explanation: 2^10 = 1024. Divide by 11: 11 × 93 = 1023, so 1024 = 11 × 93 + 1 and the remainder is 1. Modular shortcut: 2^5 = 32 ≡ −1 (mod 11), hence 2^10 ≡ (−1)² ≡ 1 (mod 11).

distractorExplanations.b: 2 is 2^1, or the remainder of 2 itself, not of 2^10.
distractorExplanations.c: 4 is the units digit of 1024, its remainder on division by 10, not by 11.
distractorExplanations.d: 10 ≡ −1 (mod 11) is 2^5’s remainder, one exponent-doubling short of 2^10.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-055.prompt: A training plan adds 5 minutes of drill each session, starting at 8 minutes in session 1. How many minutes of drill are scheduled in session 12?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-055.explanation: This is an arithmetic sequence with first term 8 and common difference 5. The 12th term is a_12 = 8 + (12 − 1) × 5 = 8 + 55 = 63 minutes. Counting 12 jumps of 5 instead of 11 is the usual off-by-one error.

distractorExplanations.a: 58 uses 10 increments (8 + 50) as if session 12 were the 11th term.
distractorExplanations.c: 68 uses 12 increments (8 + 60), one extra 5-minute step past session 12.
distractorExplanations.d: 73 uses 13 increments, matching session 14 rather than session 12.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-056.prompt: A cash account starts at $4,000 and earns 5% interest compounded once per year. What is the balance at the end of 2 years if no money is added or withdrawn?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-056.explanation: Compound growth is 4,000 × (1.05)² = 4,000 × 1.1025 = $4,410. Year 1 ends at $4,200; year 2 interest is 5% of 4,200 = $210, not another $200 on the original principal.

distractorExplanations.a: $410 is the interest earned over two years, not the ending balance.
distractorExplanations.b: $4,200 is the balance after only one year.
distractorExplanations.c: Two years of simple interest (4,000 × 0.05 × 2), missing interest on the first year’s $200.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-057.prompt: A drawer holds 5 red tags and 3 blue tags. Two tags are drawn at random with replacement, so the draws are independent. What is the probability that at least one of the two tags is red?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-057.explanation: P(red) = 5/8 and P(blue) = 3/8 on each draw. P(no red) = P(both blue) = (3/8)² = 9/64. Therefore P(at least one red) = 1 − 9/64 = 55/64. Replacement keeps the second-draw denominator at 8.

distractorExplanations.a: 25/64 is (5/8)², the chance both tags are red, which is only part of “at least one red.”
distractorExplanations.b: 30/64 is exactly one red (2 × 5/8 × 3/8); it leaves out the both-red case.
distractorExplanations.c: 40/64 = 5/8 is the chance a single draw is red, not the two-draw union.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-058.prompt: Three identical printers produce 900 pages in 6 hours, working together at a constant combined rate. At that same per-printer rate, how many hours will two of the printers take to produce 600 pages?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-058.explanation: Combined rate of three printers is 900/6 = 150 pages per hour, so one printer does 50 pages per hour. Two printers do 100 pages per hour, and 600/100 = 6 hours. The job size and crew both drop by one-third, so time is unchanged.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses the three-printer rate of 150 pages per hour (600 ÷ 150), as if all three printers still ran.
distractorExplanations.c: Scales time by 3/2 for the smaller crew but forgets that the page count also fell from 900 to 600.
distractorExplanations.d: Doubles the original 6 hours, as if two printers worked at half the speed of three.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-059.prompt: A course grade is 40% midterm and 60% final. A student scored 70 on the midterm and wants an overall grade of 82. What score is needed on the final?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-059.explanation: Solve 0.40(70) + 0.60x = 82. That is 28 + 0.60x = 82, so 0.60x = 54 and x = 90. The final is weighted more than the midterm, so it must sit above 82 to offset the 70.

distractorExplanations.a: Sets the final equal to the target grade, ignoring that the 70 midterm pulls the average down.
distractorExplanations.c: Solves 0.5(70) + 0.5x = 82, treating the weights as equal instead of 40/60.
distractorExplanations.d: Swaps the weights (60% midterm, 40% final): 42 + 0.4x = 82 gives 100.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-060.prompt: A pump fills an empty tank in 12 hours, and a drain empties the full tank in 18 hours. The pump runs alone for 4 hours, and then the drain is accidentally opened as well. How many more hours until the tank is full?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-060.explanation: After 4 hours the tank is 4/12 = 1/3 full, so 2/3 remains. With both open the net rate is 1/12 − 1/18 = 1/36 tank per hour, so the rest takes (2/3) × 36 = 24 hours.

distractorExplanations.a: Adds the rates as if the drain also filled (1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36), then applies that to the 2/3 left.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses the pump’s rate alone for the remaining 2/3 (2/3 × 12) and ignores the open drain.
distractorExplanations.d: 36 hours is the net time to fill an empty tank; the pump had already filled 1/3 of it.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-061.prompt: A linear pricing function f satisfies f(1) = 4 and f(4) = 13. If the same line is used, what is f(7)?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-061.explanation: Slope is (13 − 4)/(4 − 1) = 9/3 = 3. Then f(x) = 3x + 1, because f(1) = 3 + 1 = 4. Hence f(7) = 21 + 1 = 22. From x = 4 to x = 7 is another +3 in the input, so the output rises another 9 from 13 to 22.

distractorExplanations.a: 16 adds 3 to 13, using the slope as a raw addend instead of slope times the +3 change in x.
distractorExplanations.b: 19 adds 6 to 13, as if the run from 4 to 7 were 2 rather than 3.
distractorExplanations.c: 21 is 3 × 7 with the intercept dropped; the line is 3x + 1, not 3x.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-062.prompt: If n is a positive multiple of 4, which of the following must be a multiple of 8?

options.a: 2n
options.d: 3n

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-062.explanation: Write n = 4k for a positive integer k. Then 2n = 8k, which is always a multiple of 8. The other three expressions each fail for at least one multiple of 4, so only 2n is forced.

distractorExplanations.b: n + 4 is a multiple of 8 only when n is an odd multiple of 4 (n = 4, 12, 20, …). For n = 8, n + 4 = 12, which is not a multiple of 8.
distractorExplanations.c: n/2 is a multiple of 2, but for n = 4 it equals 2, which is not a multiple of 8.
distractorExplanations.d: 3 shares no factor with 8, so 3n is a multiple of 8 only when n already is. For n = 4, 3n = 12 is not a multiple of 8.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-063.prompt: A courier drives 120 miles at 40 mph and then another 120 miles at 60 mph. What is the courier’s average speed, in mph, for the 240-mile trip?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-063.explanation: Time on the first leg is 120/40 = 3 hours; time on the second is 120/60 = 2 hours. Total time is 5 hours for 240 miles, so average speed is 240/5 = 48 mph. Equal distances make the average the harmonic mean of 40 and 60: 2/(1/40 + 1/60) = 48, not the arithmetic mean 50.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses 40 × 60 ÷ (40 + 60) = 24, forgetting the factor 2 in the harmonic mean for two equal-distance legs.
distractorExplanations.c: Takes the geometric mean √(40 × 60) ≈ 49; average speed is total distance over total time.
distractorExplanations.d: 50 is the arithmetic mean of 40 and 60, correct only if the two legs took equal time, not equal distance.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-064.prompt: For a positive integer n, the remainder is 4 when n is divided by 9. What is the remainder when 3n + 2 is divided by 9?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-064.explanation: Write n = 9k + 4. Then 3n + 2 = 27k + 12 + 2 = 27k + 14. Since 14 = 9 + 5, the remainder is 5. Shortcut: replace n by 4 to get 3(4) + 2 = 14, and 14 leaves remainder 5 on division by 9.

distractorExplanations.a: 2 is the constant added in 3n + 2, not the remainder of the whole expression.
distractorExplanations.b: 4 is n’s remainder; multiplying by 3 and adding 2 changes the remainder.
distractorExplanations.d: 14 is 3 × 4 + 2 before dividing by 9; a remainder must be less than 9.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-065.prompt: An investment doubles in value every 8 years at a constant compound rate. If no cash is added or withdrawn, by what factor has the investment grown after 32 years?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-065.explanation: 32 years contains 32/8 = 4 doubling periods, so the growth factor is 2^4 = 16. Exponential doubling is multiplicative: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2, not 2 × 4 or 2 + 4.

distractorExplanations.a: 4 = 2² is the factor after only 16 years (two doublings), not 32.
distractorExplanations.b: 8 = 2³ is three doublings, reached at 24 years, one period short of 32.
distractorExplanations.d: 32 = 2⁵ counts one doubling too many, as if a doubling also happened at year 0.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-066.prompt: A positive number x plus its reciprocal equals 5. What is the value of x² + 1/x²?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-066.explanation: Square the given identity: (x + 1/x)² = 25 = x² + 2 + 1/x². Subtract 2 from both sides to isolate x² + 1/x² = 23. You do not need to solve for x itself.

distractorExplanations.a: Doubles 5, treating x² + 1/x² as 2(x + 1/x).
distractorExplanations.c: 25 is (x + 1/x)², which still includes the cross term 2.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the cross term 2 instead of subtracting it: 25 + 2.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-067.prompt: Inventory SKUs are integers n that leave remainder 2 when divided by 6. After the recode 4n + 1, what remainder does the new code leave on division by 6?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-067.explanation: Write n = 6k + 2. Then 4n + 1 = 24k + 8 + 1 = 24k + 9. Since 9 = 6 + 3, the remainder is 3. Shortcut: replace n by 2 to get 8 + 1 = 9, and 9 leaves remainder 3 on division by 6.

distractorExplanations.a: Multiplies n’s remainder by 4 and subtracts 1 instead of adding (8 − 1 = 7, remainder 1).
distractorExplanations.b: Drops the +1: 4 × 2 = 8 leaves remainder 2.
distractorExplanations.d: Plugs in n = 8 and reports 4n + 1 = 33 without dividing by 6; 33 leaves remainder 3.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-065-dup.prompt: A checksum keeps only the units digit of 3^27. Which units digit does it keep?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-065-dup.explanation: Units digits of powers of 3 cycle every four exponents: 3, 9, 7, 1. Because 27 = 4 × 6 + 3, the 27th power matches the third position in the cycle, which is 7. Check a small analog: 3^3 = 27, units digit 7.

distractorExplanations.a: 1 is the units digit when the exponent is a multiple of 4 (cycle position 4), and 27 is not a multiple of 4.
distractorExplanations.b: 3 is the units digit for exponents congruent to 1 mod 4, such as 3^1 or 3^25, not 3^27.
distractorExplanations.d: 9 is the units digit for exponents congruent to 2 mod 4, such as 3^2 = 9 or 3^26.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-066-dup.prompt: Three times a positive number plus 7 equals 43. If that number is then increased by 50%, what is the result?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-066-dup.explanation: Solve 3n + 7 = 43, so 3n = 36 and n = 12. Increasing 12 by 50% means 12 × 1.50 = 18. The 50% applies to n, not to 43 or to 3n.

distractorExplanations.a: 12 is the original number n; the stem then increases it by 50%.
distractorExplanations.c: Takes 50% of 43, the total in the equation, instead of increasing n.
distractorExplanations.d: Increases 3n = 36 by 50%; the stem increases the number itself, n = 12.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-067-dup.prompt: Fifteen technicians can complete a data-cleaning job in 12 days, working at the same constant rate. If the same job is instead given to 20 technicians at that same per-person rate, how many days will the job take?
gmat-focus-readiness-check-quant-067-dup.explanation: Total work is 15 × 12 = 180 technician-days. With 20 technicians the duration is 180/20 = 9 days. Worker count and days are inversely proportional when the job size is fixed: 15/20 × 12 = 9.

distractorExplanations.a: 6 days would need 30 technicians (180 ÷ 30), twice the original crew rather than 20.
distractorExplanations.b: Subtracts the 5 added technicians from 12 days; crew size and days are inversely proportional.
distractorExplanations.d: Scales by 20/15 instead of 15/20, as if more technicians needed more days.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-016.prompt: Harbor City started weekly curbside compost pickup last March. By December, methane readings at the municipal landfill had fallen 18 percent. Officials conclude that the compost program caused the drop and should be expanded citywide. Which assumption is required by the argument?

options.a: The methane decline was not wholly caused by another landfill change, such as new gas flares.
options.b: Households in every remaining ward will sort food scraps at least as carefully as households on the first routes.
options.c: Collecting compost costs the city less per ton than adding the same amount of new landfill capacity would cost.
options.d: Methane readings at landfills in neighboring cities rose over the same months that Harbor City's readings fell.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-016.explanation: The officials infer that compost pickup caused the 18 percent drop. If some other landfill change, such as new flares, fully accounted for the decline, compost caused none of it and the argument collapses (negation test). The argument needs only that the drop was not entirely due to something else, not that compost was the sole factor.

distractorExplanations.b: Sorting quality in other wards affects how well an expansion performs, but the argument survives if some wards sort less carefully, so it is not required.
distractorExplanations.c: A cost comparison could strengthen the case for expansion, yet negating it leaves the methane-cause reasoning intact, so it is not a required premise.
distractorExplanations.d: Rising methane elsewhere would strengthen the causal claim, but the argument does not depend on neighboring cities' trends; it helps without being required.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-017.prompt: After Riverton Hospital opened quiet nap rooms for night nurses, medication-dispensing errors on night shifts fell 22 percent. Administrators conclude that nap rooms improve night-shift safety. Which finding, if true, most strengthens the argument?

options.a: Day-shift nurses asked for nap rooms of their own even though their dispensing error rate was already low.
options.b: Nurses who used the rooms logged fewer microsleep lapses on wearable monitors than nurses who skipped them.
options.c: The hospital cafeteria extended its night hours and hot-meal service during the same months the rooms opened.
options.d: Night-shift hiring bonuses rose that year, bringing more newly licensed nurses onto the night dispensing roster.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-017.explanation: A physiological pathway—fewer microsleeps among actual room users—ties the rooms to alertness, which is the proposed cause of fewer errors.

distractorExplanations.a: Day-shift nurses wanting similar rooms shows demand, not that night-shift errors fell because nurses napped in them.
distractorExplanations.c: A simultaneous cafeteria change is a rival explanation for the drop, so it weakens rather than strengthens the nap-room claim.
distractorExplanations.d: More newly licensed nurses on nights would, if anything, be expected to raise dispensing errors, so this does nothing to tie the decline to nap rooms.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-018.prompt: A consulting firm reports that analysts who keep a handwritten daily planner finish more client memos than analysts who rely only on digital calendars. The firm therefore plans to require paper planners for every analyst. Which finding, if true, most weakens the plan's reasoning?

options.a: Paper planners cost more per analyst each year than the firm's current digital calendar licenses.
options.b: Several analysts who keep paper planners also use a digital calendar to book client meetings.
options.c: Productive analysts tend to prefer paper; planner use marks their drive rather than causing it.
options.d: Analysts who were given free planners last year said they enjoyed them more than their calendar app.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-018.explanation: If planner use merely tags already-productive people, forcing planners on others will not raise memo output. That selection confound undercuts the causal recommendation.

distractorExplanations.a: Cost objects to the rollout, not to the claim that planners cause higher output.
distractorExplanations.b: Using both tools does not show that planner use is a marker of drive rather than a cause of higher memo output.
distractorExplanations.d: Enjoying the planners says nothing about whether they cause higher memo output, so the inference is untouched.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-019.prompt: Every marshal at the Riverfest parade wears an orange sash. Keiko is wearing an orange sash today. Which conclusion follows from these two statements alone?

options.a: Everyone wearing an orange sash today is a Riverfest marshal, including visitors who borrowed a sash for photographs.
options.b: Keiko is serving as a marshal at the Riverfest parade because she happens to be wearing the marshals' color today.
options.c: Keiko is definitely not a marshal at the Riverfest parade merely because many non-marshals also own orange sashes.
options.d: Keiko's marshal status cannot be settled from the two statements alone.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-019.explanation: Membership implies the sash, not the reverse. A sash wearer may or may not be a marshal, so nothing about Keiko's role is entailed.

distractorExplanations.a: This illicitly converts the original conditional from marshals to all sash wearers.
distractorExplanations.b: This affirms the consequent: a sash does not prove marshal status.
distractorExplanations.c: Nothing in the premises rules Keiko out of the marshal group.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-020.prompt: Every prize-winning pastry chef I have interviewed never completed a culinary degree. Therefore, skipping culinary school raises a baker's chance of winning major prizes. Which option most accurately describes a flaw in the reasoning?

options.a: It considers only winners who skipped school, not winners with degrees or non-winners who skipped.
options.b: It overlooks that some prize-winning chefs may have trained through apprenticeships instead of degrees.
options.c: It assumes that the chefs the speaker interviewed are honest about their educational backgrounds.
options.d: It confuses winning a major prize with being admired by other pastry chefs in the industry.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-020.explanation: The speaker generalizes from a biased slice of winners and never compares base rates among degree-holders or unsuccessful dropouts, so the causal claim is unsupported.

distractorExplanations.b: Apprenticeships do not repair the missing comparison groups; the flaw is sampling only winners who skipped school.
distractorExplanations.c: Doubting the chefs' honesty attacks the data source, but even truthful answers leave the comparison-group gap.
distractorExplanations.d: The argument never equates prizes with peer admiration; the flaw is the one-sided sample of winners.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-021.prompt: Critics insist that a higher statutory wage floor must shrink manufacturing payrolls. Yet in three counties that raised the floor last year, covered-plant headcount held steady. Which finding, if true, most undermines the critics' generalization?

options.a: The three counties already had stronger manufacturing unions than the national average before the change.
options.b: Managers met the higher wage by trimming perks, not jobs, and output per worker rose.
options.c: Nearby counties that kept the old wage floor also reported fewer open factory vacancies that year.
options.d: Plant managers in the three counties publicly praised the new wage floor in local newspapers.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-021.explanation: If firms absorbed the wage through perks and productivity rather than layoffs, a higher floor need not shrink payrolls, which directly undercuts the critics' necessity claim.

distractorExplanations.a: Prior union strength could make the counties unrepresentative, which would help critics, not undercut them.
distractorExplanations.c: Fewer vacancies elsewhere is a regional labor trend; it does not show that firms absorbed the higher wage without cutting jobs.
distractorExplanations.d: Public praise is cheap talk and does not measure actual employment effects.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-022.prompt: A seed firm says its new inoculant lifts soybean yield 30 percent, citing one last-season trial on a single farm. To evaluate that claim, it would be most useful to know which of the following?

options.a: The retail price the firm intends to charge farmers per treated acre of soybeans.
options.b: Whether the host grower had used the firm's other products on different fields in past seasons.
options.c: Whether matched control acres used the standard inoculant under the same weather and soil.
options.d: How many soybean growers in the region have already placed advance orders for the inoculant.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-022.explanation: A yield jump is credible only if comparable untreated or standard-treated acres isolate the inoculant from weather and soil. A control comparison is the decisive missing fact.

distractorExplanations.a: Price speaks to adoption, not to whether the 30 percent figure is causal.
distractorExplanations.b: The grower's past purchases do not test whether the 30 percent gain was caused by the inoculant.
distractorExplanations.d: Advance orders measure demand, not whether the single-farm yield claim is valid.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-023.prompt: Unit sales of vinyl records have risen for three years while streaming subscriptions have also grown. Which finding, if true, best resolves the apparent tension?

options.a: Average streaming audio quality has improved with new codecs, making phone and speaker listening more attractive.
options.b: Entry-level turntables have become much cheaper in electronics stores over the same three years.
options.c: Several used-record shops have closed in midsize cities where vinyl collectors once concentrated.
options.d: Many subscribers buy vinyl as display objects and gifts, not as substitutes for daily streaming.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-023.explanation: If vinyl is bought for collecting and gifting while streaming covers daily listening, the two goods are complements for many buyers, so both series can rise together.

distractorExplanations.a: Better streaming quality would, if anything, pull listening away from physical discs.
distractorExplanations.b: Cheaper turntables might lift vinyl alone; they do not explain simultaneous streaming growth.
distractorExplanations.c: Shop closures would pressure vinyl sales downward, deepening rather than resolving the tension.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-024.prompt: A treasury argues that cutting the statutory rate on small-firm profits will raise total tax receipts, because owners will stop hiding cash sales. Which assumption does the argument require?

options.a: Newly reported income will more than offset the mechanical loss from applying a lower rate.
options.b: Every small firm currently conceals the entirety of its cash receipts from tax authorities.
options.c: Large corporations will not demand a matching rate cut in the next budget cycle if small-firm owners successfully lobby for the new rate.
options.d: Owners will hire extra bookkeepers once the statutory rate falls to handle the extra invoices that newly reported sales create.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-024.explanation: Receipts rise only if the extra reported base outweighs the lower rate. Without that magnitude assumption, the treasury's conclusion does not follow.

distractorExplanations.b: The argument needs some previously hidden income, not total concealment by every firm.
distractorExplanations.c: Later political demands from large firms are outside the stated revenue mechanism.
distractorExplanations.d: Bookkeeper hiring is not required for the underreporting-to-reporting story.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-025.prompt: Deep-sea ecologists mapping cobalt-rich crusts found that nodule fields host long-lived sponges whose filtration keeps near-bottom water unusually clear. In a trial strip where a collector robot removed nodules, sponge cover collapsed within months and sediment plumes drifted onto adjacent unmined plots. Filter-feeding fish then left those plots even though nodules there were untouched. Larval sponges settled slowly, and models put recovery of filtration function on the order of decades. Which statement is best supported?

options.a: Cobalt crusts and their sponge cover regenerate about as quickly as coastal oyster reefs after storms.
options.b: Nodule mining can harm filter feeders on plots the robot never scraped.
options.c: Fish abandon nearby plots only because engine noise from the collector robot scares them away for good.
options.d: Larval sponges settle faster on scraped sediment than on intact nodule pavement.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-025.explanation: Plumes reaching unmined plots, followed by fish leaving those plots, show damage beyond the scraped strip. Slow larval return supports lasting functional loss rather than quick recovery.

distractorExplanations.a: Decadal recovery models contradict a storm-fast crust rebound like oyster reefs.
distractorExplanations.c: The text ties fish exit to sediment and sponge loss, not to a permanent noise scare.
distractorExplanations.d: Slow settlement after scraping contradicts a preference for scraped sediment.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-026.prompt: Platform courier apps classify riders as independent contractors and historically left crash insurance to the riders. After several cities required platforms to carry occupational accident cover, some apps introduced per-delivery safety fees. Riders in those cities reported fewer unpaid medical bills after crashes, but weekly take-home pay fell for riders who already bought private cover. Platforms argued the fees merely passed through a legal cost; rider groups said the fees exceeded the premium increase. Which inference is most strongly supported?

options.a: Mandatory accident cover raised every rider's weekly take-home pay, including riders who already carried private crash policies.
options.b: Private insurers stopped selling accident policies to couriers once the city rules took effect.
options.c: A safety fee can leave some already-insured riders financially worse off.
options.d: Platforms introduced the fees mainly to punish riders who had organized for better pay.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-026.explanation: The passage states unpaid medical bills fell while take-home pay fell for riders who already had private cover, so the fee can harm that subgroup even if crash bills drop.

distractorExplanations.a: The already-insured group's pay drop contradicts a universal take-home gain.
distractorExplanations.b: Nothing says private insurers exited the courier market.
distractorExplanations.d: Union punishment is not mentioned; the platforms cite a legal pass-through.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-027.prompt: Desert harvester ants lay pheromone trails to seeds, but they stop reinforcing a trail when returning ants meet a jam at the nest entrance. In lab arenas, colonies facing a clogged nest switched faster to a farther seed pile than colonies with a clear entrance, even though the near pile still held food. When researchers artificially widened the entrance, the near pile was depleted first. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.a: Harvester ants abandon pheromones whenever any nestmate is injured and then ignore seed piles that still have remaining food.
options.b: The farther pile always contains more calories per seed than the near pile in the arenas.
options.c: Widening the entrance worked only because it changed how the seeds smelled to returning foragers.
options.d: Nest-entrance congestion can redirect foraging even when a near pile remains.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-027.explanation: The clogged-entrance switch to a farther pile, reversed when the entrance is widened, shows congestion itself reroutes foraging while food remains nearby.

distractorExplanations.a: Injury is never cited as the cue that stops trail reinforcement.
distractorExplanations.b: Calorie differences between piles are not reported.
distractorExplanations.c: The design changes entrance width, not seed odor, as the experimental lever.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-028.prompt: When people are given a windfall labeled 'bonus,' they spend more of it on luxuries than when the same sum is labeled 'rebate,' even though both labels describe cash already in hand. In one experiment, rebate-labeled funds were more often parked in savings accounts, while bonus-labeled funds bought restaurant meals. The pattern persisted after researchers equalized the timing of receipt. Which statement is best supported?

options.a: Mental labels on identical cash can change how readily people spend it.
options.b: Restaurant meals always yield more utility than savings account interest, so the bonus label cannot be what moved restaurant spending.
options.c: People spend rebate-labeled funds more freely than bonus-labeled funds once timing is held constant.
options.d: Windfalls raise luxury spending only when the cash arrives on a weekend rather than a weekday.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-028.explanation: Equal cash with different labels produced different spending versus saving, with timing matched, so the labels themselves shift consumption. The rebate group saved more, not less.

distractorExplanations.b: The passage reports spending patterns, not a utility ranking of meals versus interest.
distractorExplanations.c: Rebate-labeled funds were parked in savings, the opposite of spending more freely.
distractorExplanations.d: Weekend timing is not discussed; receipt timing was experimentally equalized.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-029.prompt: City-center roofs painted white reflected more sunlight than dark asphalt roofs, cutting afternoon indoor temperatures in uncooled rooms. A later trial added shallow trays of sedum on some white roofs; those plots ran cooler still, but only on dry days. After heavy rain, the planted trays stayed wet into the next afternoon and then released stored heat, erasing the extra cooling. Street-level air temperatures barely moved in either trial. Which inference is most reasonable?

options.a: White paint fails to lower indoor temperatures in any room in a dense downtown district.
options.b: Planted trays add cooling mainly in dry weather and can reverse after rain.
options.c: Street-level air temperature falls whenever rooftops across a downtown block are painted white.
options.d: Sedum trays cool roofs only because the plants make the roof surface darker than plain asphalt.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-029.explanation: The extra cooling from plants appears on dry days and disappears after rain when stored heat is released. Indoor gains from white paint still occurred; street air did not fall.

distractorExplanations.a: Uncooled rooms did run cooler after white paint, so indoor cooling is not a total failure.
distractorExplanations.c: Street-level air barely moved, so a reliable street-air drop is unsupported.
distractorExplanations.d: White plus plants is not a darkening relative to asphalt; reflectance is the point of the paint.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-030.prompt: In a pain trial, volunteers who believed they had received a strong analgesic showed reduced activity in spinal pain pathways even when the injection was saline. Telling a second group that the injection was inert produced no spinal change, although both groups had identical needles and waiting times. When the first group's belief was later reversed, spinal signals returned toward baseline. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.a: Saline injections relieve nerve-injury pain more reliably than opioid drugs do.
options.b: Needles and waiting times, not beliefs, produced the spinal change seen in the first group.
options.c: Expectancy can alter measurable spinal pain signals, not just self-report.
options.d: Reversing the first group's belief left their reduced spinal activity unchanged.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-030.explanation: Belief of analgesia changed spinal signals; an inert-label group with the same needle did not; reversing belief moved signals back. That pattern isolates expectancy from the injection itself.

distractorExplanations.a: The study does not compare saline with opioids as treatments for nerve injury.
distractorExplanations.b: Matched needles without the belief produced no spinal change, so hardware is not the cause.
distractorExplanations.d: The reversal condition moved signals toward baseline, contradicting 'never restores'.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-verbal-016.prompt: Historians of inland transport note that nineteenth-century canal companies often lobbied against early railways, claiming trains would devastate farm prices by flooding markets. In districts where rails arrived first, however, dairy output rose because milk could reach cities before spoiling. Canal tonnage in those districts later recovered by shifting to coal and grain, goods that tolerate slower hauls. Passenger coaches on canals collapsed and did not return. Which statement is best supported?

options.a: Railways reduced every type of canal cargo to zero within a single season of opening.
options.b: Dairy farmers opposed railways more fiercely than canal shareholders did in the districts where rails arrived before the canals did.
options.c: Coal and grain spoiled about as quickly as milk when hauled on warm canal barges.
options.d: Rails could complement canals by taking time-sensitive goods while slow bulk stayed on water.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-verbal-016.explanation: Dairy growth plus later canal recovery in coal and grain, alongside lost passenger traffic, shows a split: speed-sensitive goods moved to rail while bulk stayed. Total canal collapse is denied by the recovery.

distractorExplanations.a: Later recovery in coal and grain contradicts a total, immediate zeroing of canal cargo.
distractorExplanations.b: The passage never ranks dairy farmers' lobbying against shareholders'.
distractorExplanations.c: Coal and grain are cited as tolerant of slow hauls, the opposite of milk-like spoilage.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-verbal-017.prompt: Excavators at a highland pass recovered drilled marine-shell beads in layers dated centuries before local agriculture. The nearest shore lies several weeks' walk away, and the beads' drill-hole wear matches pieces found in a coastal cemetery of the same period. Animal-bone collagen from the highland hearths shows no marine diet. A few unfinished bead blanks appear only at the coast, not at the pass. Which inference is best supported?

options.a: Finished ornaments reached the pass through exchange, not through a coastal diet.
options.b: Highland foragers harvested shellfish themselves during seasonal camps on the distant shore.
options.c: Bead blanks were manufactured at the highland pass and later carried down to the coast.
options.d: The coastal cemetery dates to many centuries after the beaded highland layers were deposited.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-verbal-017.explanation: Wear-matched coastal beads inland, no marine diet, and blanks only at the coast together indicate finished goods traveling uphill, not local shellfishing or highland manufacture.

distractorExplanations.b: Absent marine collagen argues against highlanders eating shellfish from sea camps.
distractorExplanations.c: Blanks only at the coast contradict manufacture at the pass.
distractorExplanations.d: The text dates beads and cemetery to the same period, not a later cemetery.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-verbal-018.prompt: Employees who join a firm's optional lunchtime yoga series report fewer migraine days than employees who never join. The wellness director concludes that yoga reduces migraines and wants to make the series mandatory. Which finding, if true, most weakens that conclusion?

options.a: The yoga instructor is especially popular with employees who belong to the firm's social club.
options.b: Joiners already had fewer migraines and better sleep before the series began.
options.c: The studio space could hold only half the workforce at once, so making the series mandatory would still need extra rooms.
options.d: Several nearby firms offer discounted gym memberships to employees instead of yoga classes.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-verbal-018.explanation: If joiners were already healthier, the migraine gap is selection, not a treatment effect, so mandating yoga would not be justified by these numbers.

distractorExplanations.a: Instructor popularity might explain attendance, not the migraine comparison's causal meaning.
distractorExplanations.c: Room capacity is a logistics limit, not a confounder of who reports fewer migraines.
distractorExplanations.d: Other firms' gym perks do not explain this firm's joiner-versus-nonjoiner gap.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-verbal-019.prompt: A nutrition newsletter claims that drinking two cups of matcha daily raises scores on a working-memory task, citing volunteers who already consumed matcha and outscored abstainers. Which finding, if true, most weakens the causal claim?

options.a: A daily serving of ceremonial-grade matcha costs several times more than a cup of supermarket black tea.
options.b: Some volunteers disliked the grassy taste of ceremonial-grade powder and drank it less often.
options.c: Matcha drinkers also slept longer and practiced meditation, both independently linked to memory scores.
options.d: The working-memory task asked volunteers to recall sequences of shapes rather than lists of words.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-verbal-019.explanation: Sleep and meditation are alternate causes that can produce the score gap without matcha being responsible, which undercuts the newsletter's causal leap.

distractorExplanations.a: Price does not explain why drinkers outscored abstainers on the task.
distractorExplanations.b: Taste dislike would, if anything, reduce consumption, not create a spurious memory benefit.
distractorExplanations.d: The stimulus type does not itself introduce a confound between drinkers and abstainers.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-verbal-020.prompt: Clearwater's council says a new waterfront arena will revive nearby shop rents because visiting fans will linger on the promenade. Which assumption is required?

options.a: Construction of the arena will be finished before the next municipal election takes place.
options.b: Nearby shop owners already sell team merchandise and souvenirs in their current storefronts.
options.c: Hotel occupancy downtown has fallen for three consecutive summers despite new tourism marketing.
options.d: A substantial share of fans will spend time and money on the promenade, not just in the arena.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-verbal-020.explanation: Rent revival via promenade lingering requires that fans actually exit onto the promenade and spend. If they stay inside, the council's mechanism fails.

distractorExplanations.a: The election calendar is politically relevant but not required for the rent mechanism.
distractorExplanations.b: Existing merchandise sales are not needed for the fan-lingering story.
distractorExplanations.c: Hotel occupancy is a separate downtown indicator, not a premise of promenade spending.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-verbal-021.prompt: A school board wants to drop an end-of-year writing exam because scores correlate weakly with later college grades. Which finding, if true, most strengthens the board's plan?

options.a: The exam mainly rewards handwriting speed, a skill college seminars rarely grade.
options.b: Parents in the district generally prefer multiple-choice tests to essays when the board discusses whether to keep the writing exam.
options.c: Several nearby districts still administer a similar end-of-year writing exam every spring.
options.d: Each exam is scored by two teachers, and their scores occasionally differ by a point.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-verbal-021.explanation: If the exam measures a skill colleges do not use, weak correlation is expected and dropping it is more justified than if it measured valued writing.

distractorExplanations.b: Parental format preference is not evidence that the exam fails as a college signal.
distractorExplanations.c: Neighboring practice does not show this exam is a poor measure.
distractorExplanations.d: Minor scorer disagreement is a reliability detail; it does not show that the exam measures a skill colleges ignore.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-verbal-022.prompt: Conservationists long treated habitat fencing as the default for a rare grassland bird. A new field program moved eggs to predator-free islands; fledging rates there exceeded fenced mainland nests, but returning adults later failed to find mates because island choruses were too small. Geneticists warn that a few island lineages could dominate. Which statement is best supported?

options.a: Fencing mainland nests always produces more fledglings than moving eggs to islands.
options.b: Raising fledging success can still leave a population demographically fragile.
options.c: Island choruses grew large enough to give every returning adult a good chance of finding a mate.
options.d: Geneticists now recommend replacing all mainland habitat protection with island colonies.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-verbal-022.explanation: Higher fledging with later mate shortage and lineage-dominance risk shows that a nest-success gain can still leave a fragile population. Mainland fencing is not shown to be universally worse.

distractorExplanations.a: Island fledging exceeded fenced mainland nests, so fencing is not always superior.
distractorExplanations.c: Adults failed to find mates because choruses were too small, contradicting a guarantee.
distractorExplanations.d: The genetic warning is about lineage dominance, not a call to abandon all mainland habitat.

gmat-focus-readiness-check-verbal-023.prompt: Office workers who bring a standing mat report less afternoon back tightness than workers who sit all day. Facilities concludes that mats cause the relief and will buy one for every desk. Which finding, if true, most weakens that conclusion?

options.a: Standing mats wear out and must be replaced more often than standard chair mats.
options.b: Several workers already owned a standing mat from a previous employer before the study began.
options.c: Mat users also take more short walking breaks, a habit independently tied to less tightness.
